t: Strings Differ by One Character - From Pairwise Scans to Wildcard Hashing
o: Every word in dict has the same length m, and we must decide whether some pair differs in exactly one position. A useful restatement: two unique equal-length words differ in exactly one spot if and only if blanking out that spot in both yields the same wildcard pattern - abcd and aacd both become a*cd. The constraints cap the total number of characters at 10^5, so n times m is bounded even though n alone can be huge. That rules out naive O(n^2 * m) pairwise checking for many short words, and motivates hashing the wildcard patterns instead.
k: Two unique equal-length strings differ at exactly one index iff their masked copies (that index replaced by *) are identical.
Masks produced by the same word can never collide, because the * sits at a different offset in each mask.
Prefix and suffix rolling hashes assemble every mask of a word in O(1) each, cutting the mask-construction cost.

a.i: The most literal solution: check every unordered pair of words and count mismatched positions, answering true at the first pair with exactly one mismatch. Breaking out of the inner loop once two mismatches appear keeps the common case fast. With up to roughly n^2/2 pairs this is fine on small inputs but degrades badly when dict holds many short words, so treat it as the intuitive baseline.
s: Iterate over all pairs (i, j) with i less than j.
Count differing positions between dict[i] and dict[j], aborting once the count exceeds one.
Return true if a pair finishes with exactly one difference.
Return false after exhausting all pairs.
a.t: O(n^2 * m) - every pair costs up to m character comparisons.
a.sp: O(1) - only mismatch counters beyond the input.

a.i: For each word generate its m masks, each with one position replaced by *, and insert them all into a hash set. Because the words themselves are unique, a repeated mask can only come from two different words agreeing everywhere except the starred slot - exactly the condition we want. Masks from the same word never collide since the star lands at different indices, so no extra position bookkeeping is needed. Each mask costs O(m) to build and hash, giving quadratic-in-m behavior that still fits the 10^5-character budget.
s: Create an empty hash set of mask strings.
For each word and each index i, build the mask with * at position i.
If the mask already exists in the set, return true.
Otherwise insert it; return false once every mask is processed.
a.t: O(n * m^2) - m masks per word, each of length m to build and hash.
a.sp: O(n * m^2) - up to n*m stored masks of length m, safely bounded since n*m is at most 10^5.

a.i: Replace explicit mask strings with numbers. For each word precompute polynomial prefix hashes pre[i] of the first i letters and suffix hashes suf[i+1] of the letters after position i; then the mask with the star at position i has hash pre[i] times B^(m-i) plus suf[i+1], treating the star as value 0, all in O(1). Combining two independent moduli into one composite key makes accidental collisions astronomically unlikely. Overall cost drops to O(n * m), which is optimal since every character must be read at least once.
s: Precompute powers of a base B modulo two primes M1 and M2 up to m.
For each word, compute prefix hashes and suffix polynomial hashes under both moduli.
For each i, combine pre[i], an implicit zero for the star, and suf[i+1] into a double-hash key.
Return true if a key repeats; otherwise return false.

c.python:
class Solution:
    def differByOne(self, d: List[str]) -> bool:
        MOD1, MOD2, B = 1_000_000_007, 998_244_353, 131
        m = len(d[0])
        p1 = [1] * (m + 1)
        p2 = [1] * (m + 1)
        for i in range(m):
            p1[i + 1] = p1[i] * B % MOD1
            p2[i + 1] = p2[i] * B % MOD2
        seen = set()
        for w in d:
            a1 = [0] * (m + 1)
            a2 = [0] * (m + 1)
            for i in range(m):
                c = ord(w[i])
                a1[i + 1] = (a1[i] * B + c) % MOD1
                a2[i + 1] = (a2[i] * B + c) % MOD2
            s1 = [0] * (m + 1)
            s2 = [0] * (m + 1)
            for i in range(m - 1, -1, -1):
                c = ord(w[i])
                s1[i] = (c * p1[m - 1 - i] + s1[i + 1]) % MOD1
                s2[i] = (c * p2[m - 1 - i] + s2[i + 1]) % MOD2
            for i in range(m):
                key = ((a1[i] * p1[m - i] + s1[i + 1]) % MOD1,
                       (a2[i] * p2[m - i] + s2[i + 1]) % MOD2)
                if key in seen:
                    return True
                seen.add(key)
        return False

a.t: O(n * m) - constant-time hash assembly per (word, position) pair.
a.sp: O(n * m) - one composite key stored per (word, position).

w: State the brute force first to show you understand the matching condition, then switch to the mask hash set, which is the sweet spot of simplicity and speed for these constraints; bring up rolling hashes only if the interviewer pushes for linear time. Pitfalls: relying on uniqueness of the words (the collision-means-answer argument depends on it) and using a single small modulus, which invites collisions. A subtle point worth voicing: the star position is encoded in the mask itself, so cross-position comparisons are safe. Follow-ups: return the actual pair (store a word id next to each mask), or generalize to words of differing lengths by bucketing on length first.
